name: Fitness AI Starter Evidence Cards
description: A manually curated starter RAG knowledge base based on six high-priority sources. Each card contains one narrow claim and practical app-safe guidance.

reviewPolicy.reviewInterval: Review every 6 to 12 months, and earlier when a major guideline is updated.
reviewPolicy.importantNote: These cards provide general educational information. They must not be used as a medical diagnosis, medical clearance, rehabilitation prescription, or substitute for a qualified professional.

cards.claim: Consistent progressive resistance training improves muscular strength, muscle size, power, and physical function in healthy adults.
practicalAdvice: Prioritize a routine the user can follow consistently.
Increase the challenge gradually over time instead of making large jumps.
Use the user's goal, experience, enjoyment, and recovery to guide the plan.

source.title: Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults: An Overview of Reviews
source.scope: Healthy adults; resistance-training prescription for strength, hypertrophy, power, muscular endurance, and physical function.

contraindications: Do not use this card as a medical clearance tool.
Do not advise training through sharp pain or acute injury symptoms.
limitations: The best plan depends on the user's goal and ability to recover; one fixed routine is not optimal for everyone.

cards.claim: Resistance-training programs should be individualized rather than treated as one-size-fits-all.
practicalAdvice: Ask the user about their main goal: general health, strength, muscle growth, or sports performance.
Start with a realistic schedule the user can maintain.
Adjust exercises, volume, and load when the current plan is too difficult to recover from or too easy to progress with.

source.title: Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults: An Overview of Reviews
source.scope: Healthy adults; resistance-training prescription for strength, hypertrophy, power, muscular endurance, and physical function.

limitations: General guidance should not replace individualized medical, rehabilitation, or sports-performance programming.

cards.claim: For muscle growth, a higher weekly resistance-training volume can be useful; the ACSM summary gives about 10 sets per muscle group per week as a practical target.
practicalAdvice: Treat about 10 weekly sets per muscle group as a general starting target, not a strict rule.
Spread the work across manageable sessions when helpful.
Increase or reduce volume based on training experience, performance trends, soreness, and recovery.

source.title: Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults: An Overview of Reviews
source.scope: Healthy adults; resistance-training prescription for strength, hypertrophy, power, muscular endurance, and physical function.

dosage.setsPerWeek: Around 10 sets per muscle group per week is a practical general target for hypertrophy; adjust individually.

contraindications: Reduce volume and review the plan if performance decreases persistently or recovery is poor.
limitations: A weekly set target is a starting point. Exercise selection, effort, recovery, and adherence still matter.

applicablePopulation: healthy adults with appropriate technique and experience
cards.claim: For maximizing strength, heavier resistance can be emphasized. The ACSM summary highlights loads around 80% of one-repetition maximum for 2 to 3 sets per exercise.
practicalAdvice: Use heavier loads only when the user can maintain controlled technique.
Progress gradually instead of testing maximal lifts frequently.
For beginners, prioritize technique and consistent practice before advanced loading strategies.

source.title: Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults: An Overview of Reviews
source.scope: Healthy adults; resistance-training prescription for strength, hypertrophy, power, muscular endurance, and physical function.

dosage.intensity: Around 80% of 1RM can be emphasized for strength-oriented training.
dosage.setsPerWeek: The ACSM summary describes 2 to 3 sets per exercise for strength-oriented work.

contraindications: Do not use near-maximal loading advice for unsupervised minors.
Do not recommend heavy lifting through pain or after an acute injury.
limitations: This is a broad strength-focused prescription, not a personalized lifting plan.

cards.claim: Power-oriented resistance training uses moderate loads and emphasizes moving the weight quickly during the lifting phase while maintaining control.
practicalAdvice: Use power work only after the user has learned safe technique.
Keep repetitions controlled and stop when speed or form declines.
Use qualified supervision for youth, beginners, or users with medical concerns.

source.title: Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults: An Overview of Reviews
source.scope: Healthy adults; resistance-training prescription for strength, hypertrophy, power, muscular endurance, and physical function.

dosage.intensity: The ACSM summary highlights approximately 30% to 70% of 1RM for power training.

contraindications: Avoid unsupervised explosive training for inexperienced users.
Stop if the user reports pain, dizziness, or loss of control.
limitations: Power training should be scaled to the user's skill level and exercise choice.

cards.claim: Traditional gym equipment is not required for useful resistance training. Bodyweight exercises, elastic bands, and home-based routines can still improve outcomes.
practicalAdvice: Offer home-based alternatives when the user does not have gym access.
Choose exercises that can be performed safely with available equipment.
Progress by improving technique, adding repetitions, using a harder variation, or gradually adding resistance.

source.title: Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults: An Overview of Reviews
source.scope: Healthy adults; resistance-training prescription for strength, hypertrophy, power, muscular endurance, and physical function.

cards.claim: Training to complete muscular failure is not consistently necessary for the average healthy adult to gain benefits from resistance training.
practicalAdvice: Do not tell users to push every set until they cannot complete another repetition.
Encourage stopping a set when technique becomes unstable.
Use harder sets selectively when appropriate for the user's experience and recovery.

source.title: Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults: An Overview of Reviews
source.scope: Healthy adults; resistance-training prescription for strength, hypertrophy, power, muscular endurance, and physical function.

contraindications: Do not recommend repeated all-out efforts when the user has poor recovery, pain, or unsafe technique.
limitations: Advanced trainees may use effort-management strategies differently depending on their goal.

cards.claim: Complex training techniques are often optional for general health and fitness. A simple, maintainable program can still be effective.
practicalAdvice: Start beginners with a simple plan that is easy to follow.
Add complexity only when it solves a clear problem, such as stalled progress or a sports-specific need.
Do not overwhelm users with advanced methods when consistency is the main issue.

source.title: Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults: An Overview of Reviews
source.scope: Healthy adults; resistance-training prescription for strength, hypertrophy, power, muscular endurance, and physical function.

cards.claim: Any amount of physical activity is better than none, and all physical activity counts.
practicalAdvice: Encourage users to start with realistic increases in activity.
Avoid framing exercise as all-or-nothing.
Suggest simple activity options such as walking, cycling, active recreation, or age-appropriate exercise.

source.title: WHO Guidelines on Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour
source.scope: Population-level physical-activity and sedentary-behaviour guidance across age groups and selected special populations.

limitations: This is general public-health guidance, not a medical exercise prescription.

cards.claim: Adults should generally aim for 150 to 300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity per week, or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous-intensity activity, or an equivalent combination.
practicalAdvice: Let users accumulate activity across the week.
Scale the starting amount to the user's current activity level.
Increase activity gradually when the user is inactive or returning after a break.

source.title: WHO Guidelines on Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour
source.scope: Population-level physical-activity and sedentary-behaviour guidance across age groups and selected special populations.

dosage.intensity: 150–300 minutes moderate intensity, or 75–150 minutes vigorous intensity, or an equivalent combination.

contraindications: Users with symptoms, medical restrictions, or major health concerns should follow professional advice.

cards.claim: Adults should perform muscle-strengthening activities involving major muscle groups on 2 or more days per week.
practicalAdvice: Include major muscle groups across the weekly plan.
Use a beginner-friendly routine when the user is new to resistance training.
Treat two days per week as a practical health baseline rather than a bodybuilding requirement.

source.title: WHO Guidelines on Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour
source.scope: Population-level physical-activity and sedentary-behaviour guidance across age groups and selected special populations.

dosage.frequency: 2 or more days per week involving major muscle groups.

limitations: Training frequency for specific fitness goals may be adjusted beyond the public-health baseline.

cards.claim: Children and adolescents aged 5 to 17 should average at least 60 minutes per day of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity across the week, with vigorous aerobic activity and muscle- and bone-strengthening activity included at least 3 days per week.
practicalAdvice: Keep youth recommendations age-appropriate, enjoyable, and varied.
Encourage movement and skill-building rather than extreme routines.
Use supervision and proper technique for structured resistance training.

source.title: WHO Guidelines on Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour
source.scope: Population-level physical-activity and sedentary-behaviour guidance across age groups and selected special populations.

dosage.frequency: Average of at least 60 minutes per day across the week; muscle- and bone-strengthening activities at least 3 days per week.

contraindications: Do not generate aggressive weight-loss or bodybuilding-style plans for minors.
Use the AAP youth-safety cards for structured resistance training.
limitations: This is population-level guidance. Individual sports training needs can vary.

cards.claim: Older adults should include multicomponent physical activity emphasizing functional balance and strength training on 3 or more days per week to support function and reduce fall risk.
practicalAdvice: Use simple, stable movements appropriate to the user's ability.
Prioritize safe progression and balance support where needed.
Recommend professional guidance when the user has fall risk, frailty, or medical limitations.

source.title: WHO Guidelines on Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour
source.scope: Population-level physical-activity and sedentary-behaviour guidance across age groups and selected special populations.

dosage.frequency: Functional balance and strength-focused multicomponent activity on 3 or more days per week.

contraindications: Do not provide unsupervised fall-risk exercises to users reporting instability or recent falls.

cards.claim: People of all age groups should limit sedentary time and replace some of it with physical activity when possible.
practicalAdvice: Encourage short movement breaks during long periods of sitting.
Suggest gradual changes rather than unrealistic daily targets.
Treat movement breaks as additions to, not replacements for, an overall activity plan.

source.title: WHO Guidelines on Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour
source.scope: Population-level physical-activity and sedentary-behaviour guidance across age groups and selected special populations.

cards.claim: Sports-nutrition advice should be individualized. Personalized plans are best handled by a qualified registered dietitian nutritionist, especially when needs are complex.
practicalAdvice: Give general educational guidance in the app.
Avoid presenting a generated meal plan as a medical or clinical prescription.
Recommend professional support for complex goals, health conditions, suspected deficiencies, or disordered-eating risk.

source.title: Nutrition and Athletic Performance
source.organization: Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, Dietitians of Canada, and American College of Sports Medicine
source.scope: Nutrition factors that influence athletic performance; emphasizes individualized planning and referral to a qualified dietitian for personalized plans.

escalationRules: Escalate when the user has a medical condition, persistent symptoms, suspected nutrient deficiency, pregnancy, or disordered-eating risk language.

cards.claim: Adequate energy intake supports training, recovery, health, and performance. A nutrition plan should avoid chronic under-fueling.
practicalAdvice: Do not recommend extreme calorie restriction.
Use small, sustainable adjustments when discussing body-composition goals.
Review training performance, energy, recovery, and hunger trends instead of focusing only on body weight.

source.title: Nutrition and Athletic Performance
source.organization: Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, Dietitians of Canada, and American College of Sports Medicine
source.scope: Nutrition factors that influence athletic performance; emphasizes individualized planning and referral to a qualified dietitian for personalized plans.

contraindications: Avoid aggressive calorie-deficit advice for minors.
Do not encourage skipping meals or compensatory exercise.
escalationRules: Escalate if the user reports persistent fatigue, dizziness, frequent injuries, major performance decline, or restrictive eating patterns.
limitations: Exact calorie needs require individualized assessment.

cards.claim: Carbohydrate intake is an important part of fueling training and athletic performance, especially when activity demands are high.
practicalAdvice: Encourage users to include carbohydrate-containing foods as part of balanced meals.
Increase attention to fueling when training volume or intensity is high.
Avoid describing carbohydrates as automatically harmful.

source.title: Nutrition and Athletic Performance
source.organization: Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, Dietitians of Canada, and American College of Sports Medicine
source.scope: Nutrition factors that influence athletic performance; emphasizes individualized planning and referral to a qualified dietitian for personalized plans.

limitations: The appropriate amount varies with sport, training load, body size, and overall diet.

cards.claim: Hydration should be considered as part of training and recovery because fluid needs can affect health and performance.
practicalAdvice: Encourage regular fluid intake across the day.
Remind users that needs vary with activity duration, sweating, heat, and individual factors.
Use caution when the user reports symptoms during exercise.

source.title: Nutrition and Athletic Performance
source.organization: Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, Dietitians of Canada, and American College of Sports Medicine
source.scope: Nutrition factors that influence athletic performance; emphasizes individualized planning and referral to a qualified dietitian for personalized plans.

escalationRules: Escalate when the user reports fainting, confusion, severe weakness, or concerning exercise-related symptoms.

cards.claim: A balanced eating pattern should be the foundation of sports nutrition. Supplements should not replace adequate food intake.
practicalAdvice: Prioritize regular meals and nutrient-dense foods.
Treat supplements as optional and context-dependent, not as the starting point.
Avoid unsupported supplement claims.

source.title: Nutrition and Athletic Performance
source.organization: Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, Dietitians of Canada, and American College of Sports Medicine
source.scope: Nutrition factors that influence athletic performance; emphasizes individualized planning and referral to a qualified dietitian for personalized plans.

limitations: Specific deficiencies or clinical nutrition issues require professional assessment.

cards.claim: In healthy adults performing prolonged resistance training, protein supplementation can modestly improve gains in muscle size and strength.
practicalAdvice: Emphasize that resistance training remains the main stimulus.
Treat protein supplements as a convenient option, not a requirement.
Encourage food-based protein sources when practical.

source.title: A Systematic Review, Meta-analysis and Meta-regression of the Effect of Protein Supplementation on Resistance Training-induced Gains in Muscle Mass and Strength in Healthy Adults
source.scope: Healthy adults performing resistance exercise training for at least 6 weeks; protein supplementation and training adaptations.

excludedPopulation: children and adolescents unless reviewed separately
limitations: The review studied healthy adults and supplementation during resistance training lasting at least 6 weeks.

cards.claim: For healthy adults performing resistance training, benefits from higher protein intake appear to level off around a total daily intake of approximately 1.6 grams per kilogram of body weight per day.
practicalAdvice: Treat approximately 1.6 g/kg/day as a useful evidence-based reference point for healthy adults, not a mandatory target for everyone.
Avoid pushing protein intake higher without a clear reason.
Consider the user's overall diet and medical context.

source.title: A Systematic Review, Meta-analysis and Meta-regression of the Effect of Protein Supplementation on Resistance Training-induced Gains in Muscle Mass and Strength in Healthy Adults
source.scope: Healthy adults performing resistance exercise training for at least 6 weeks; protein supplementation and training adaptations.

dosage.protein: Approximately 1.6 g/kg/day is a useful reference point for healthy adults doing resistance training; higher intake did not further contribute to fat-free-mass gains in the meta-regression.

contraindications: Do not provide a personalized protein prescription when the user reports a medical condition requiring dietary management.
excludedPopulation: users with kidney disease or other medical nutrition restrictions
limitations: This value is a population-level reference from a meta-regression, not an exact requirement for every individual.

cards.claim: Protein supplements are optional. They can help users reach an appropriate daily intake, but they are not required when sufficient protein is obtained from food.
practicalAdvice: Recommend food-first options when practical.
Describe supplements as a convenience rather than a shortcut.
Avoid recommending products or doses to minors without appropriate adult and professional guidance.

source.title: A Systematic Review, Meta-analysis and Meta-regression of the Effect of Protein Supplementation on Resistance Training-induced Gains in Muscle Mass and Strength in Healthy Adults
source.scope: Healthy adults performing resistance exercise training for at least 6 weeks; protein supplementation and training adaptations.

limitations: The review evaluated supplementation; it does not mean supplements are superior to an adequate food-based diet.

cards.claim: Children and adolescents can gain strength with low injury rates when resistance training is well supervised and emphasizes correct technique.
practicalAdvice: Use technique-first language for youth.
Recommend qualified supervision.
Use age-appropriate exercises and gradual progression.
Avoid unsupervised maximal-lifting advice.

source.title: Resistance Training for Children and Adolescents
source.scope: Children and adolescents; benefits, safety, supervision, technique, progression, and conditions that require medical consultation.

contraindications: Do not generate advanced or maximal-strength testing instructions for unsupervised minors.
limitations: Program design should account for the young person's skill competency, goals, and training experience.

cards.claim: Youth resistance training is not limited to lifting heavy weights. It can use bodyweight movements, bands, machines, free weights, medicine balls, kettlebells, and other appropriate resistance modes.
practicalAdvice: Choose age-appropriate exercises the user can perform with control.
Start with technique and movement quality.
Select equipment that fits the user's size and skill level.

source.title: Resistance Training for Children and Adolescents
source.scope: Children and adolescents; benefits, safety, supervision, technique, progression, and conditions that require medical consultation.

contraindications: Do not suggest equipment the minor cannot use safely or without supervision.

cards.claim: Well-designed resistance-training programs have not been shown to harm growth-plate health, linear growth, or cardiovascular health in youth.
practicalAdvice: Correct the myth that all resistance training automatically stunts growth.
Still emphasize safe supervision, correct technique, and appropriate progression.
Do not use this statement to dismiss pain, injury, or medical concerns.

source.title: Resistance Training for Children and Adolescents
source.scope: Children and adolescents; benefits, safety, supervision, technique, progression, and conditions that require medical consultation.

limitations: This applies to well-designed programs, not unsafe lifting practices.

cards.claim: Resistance training should be counted as part of a young person's total training load to reduce the risk of overuse injuries.
practicalAdvice: Consider sports practice, physical education, games, and resistance training together.
Avoid adding a demanding gym program on top of an already heavy schedule without recovery.
Encourage rest and review the plan when soreness, fatigue, or performance decline persists.

source.title: Resistance Training for Children and Adolescents
source.scope: Children and adolescents; benefits, safety, supervision, technique, progression, and conditions that require medical consultation.

escalationRules: Recommend consultation when the user reports persistent pain, repeated injuries, or significant performance decline.

cards.claim: Some health situations require medical consultation before a young person starts or continues a resistance-training program.
practicalAdvice: Keep the app's advice general when a minor reports a medical condition.
Recommend consultation with a qualified medical professional.
Do not attempt to clear the user for exercise.

source.title: Resistance Training for Children and Adolescents
source.scope: Children and adolescents; benefits, safety, supervision, technique, progression, and conditions that require medical consultation.

escalationRules: Escalate when a minor reports a known medical condition, concerning symptoms, or a history of significant injury.
limitations: The app must not diagnose conditions or decide whether a minor is medically cleared to train.

applicablePopulation: physically active users at risk of under-fueling
cards.claim: Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport, or REDs, is a syndrome of impaired physiological and/or psychological functioning associated with problematic low energy availability. It can affect female and male athletes.
practicalAdvice: Use REDs-aware language when discussing calorie deficits with active users.
Avoid normalizing chronic under-fueling.
Explain that health and performance can be affected when training demands are not matched with adequate energy intake.

source.title: 2023 International Olympic Committee's (IOC) Consensus Statement on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs)
source.scope: Female and male athletes; health and performance consequences associated with problematic low energy availability.

limitations: The app cannot diagnose REDs.

cards.claim: Aggressive or prolonged energy restriction can create health and performance risks, especially for active users.
practicalAdvice: Do not generate extreme calorie-deficit plans.
Do not encourage skipping meals, compensatory exercise, or rapid weight-loss strategies.
Prefer sustainable, cautious language for body-composition goals.

source.title: 2023 International Olympic Committee's (IOC) Consensus Statement on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs)
source.scope: Female and male athletes; health and performance consequences associated with problematic low energy availability.

contraindications: Do not provide aggressive weight-loss guidance to minors.
Do not continue detailed dieting advice when disordered-eating risk language appears.
escalationRules: Recommend professional support when restrictive eating, persistent under-fueling, or concerning symptoms are reported.

cards.claim: Persistent fatigue, reduced recovery, declining performance, or repeated injuries may be reasons to stop giving routine fitness advice and recommend professional evaluation.
practicalAdvice: Respond with a safety-focused message rather than a harder training plan.
Encourage the user to speak with a qualified healthcare professional or sports dietitian.
Avoid diagnosing the cause based only on chat messages.

source.title: 2023 International Olympic Committee's (IOC) Consensus Statement on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs)
source.scope: Female and male athletes; health and performance consequences associated with problematic low energy availability.

escalationRules: Escalate for persistent fatigue, repeated injuries, major performance decline, concerning restrictive eating patterns, or other ongoing symptoms.
limitations: These signs can have multiple causes. The app should not diagnose REDs or any medical condition.

cards.claim: For minors, the app should avoid detailed calorie-cutting prescriptions and prioritize healthy fueling, safe activity, and support from a parent or qualified professional when needed.
practicalAdvice: Use general healthy-eating guidance for minors.
Avoid numerical calorie-deficit targets for minors.
Encourage adult and professional support for significant body-composition goals or concerning symptoms.

source.title: 2023 International Olympic Committee's (IOC) Consensus Statement on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs)
source.scope: Female and male athletes; health and performance consequences associated with problematic low energy availability.

contraindications: Do not generate restrictive diets, rapid weight-loss targets, or compensatory-exercise plans for minors.
escalationRules: Escalate when a minor expresses restrictive eating patterns, persistent fatigue, dizziness, repeated injuries, or major body-image distress.
limitations: This is a protective app rule informed by REDs safety principles, not a diagnosis.

cards.claim: 7-9 hours of sleep supports muscle protein synthesis and anabolic hormone balance.
practicalAdvice: Aim for 7 to 9 hours of sleep to optimize recovery and muscle building.
Consistent sleep schedules help regulate hormones necessary for training adaptation.

source.title: WHO Guidelines on Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour
source.scope: Population-level guidance.

cards.claim: Acute dehydration exceeding 2% of body mass has been shown to reduce strength and endurance output.
practicalAdvice: Maintain adequate hydration by drinking water consistently throughout the day.
Dehydration can decrease power output and make workouts feel harder.

source.title: Nutrition and Athletic Performance
source.scope: Nutrition factors that influence performance.

cards.claim: Chronic sleep restriction elevates cortisol and reduces testosterone, impairing the anabolic response to resistance training.
practicalAdvice: Prioritize sleep duration when training load is high to mitigate stress hormones.
Sleep deprivation impairs muscle repair and strength recovery after heavy training.

source.title: WHO Guidelines on Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour
source.scope: Population-level guidance.

cards.claim: Sleep restriction can negatively impact cognitive function and may impair specific aspects of physical performance, immunity, and recovery.
practicalAdvice: Prioritize consistent sleep to maintain cognitive focus and support optimal exercise recovery.
Avoid accumulating sleep debt, especially during periods of heavy training.

source.title: Sleep and athletic performance: the effects of sleep loss on exercise performance, and physiological and cognitive responses to exercise
source.scope: Athletes; impact of sleep loss on exercise and cognitive performance.

cards.claim: Extending sleep to 10 hours per night can significantly improve athletic performance metrics such as sprint speed, shooting accuracy, and reaction time in athletes.
practicalAdvice: If training volume is high or you are preparing for competition, try to extend your sleep duration to maximize physical and mental readiness.
More sleep directly translates to improved performance and reduced fatigue.

source.title: The effects of sleep extension on the athletic performance of collegiate basketball players
source.scope: Collegiate basketball players; effects of extended sleep on athletic performance.

dosage.note: A target of 9-10 hours in bed was used to achieve these specific performance benefits.

cards.claim: Creatine monohydrate is a safe, effective, and well-tolerated nutritional ergogenic aid for enhancing high-intensity exercise performance and training adaptations.
practicalAdvice: A daily dose of 3-5 grams of creatine monohydrate is effective for maintaining elevated muscle creatine stores over time.
It is one of the most researched supplements and is safe for long-term use in healthy individuals.

source.title: International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand: safety and efficacy of creatine supplementation in exercise, sport, and medicine
source.organization: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition
source.scope: Athletes and general population; safety and efficacy of creatine.

dosage.note: Standard maintenance dose is 3-5 g/day. A loading phase (e.g., 20 g/day for 5-7 days) is optional for faster saturation.

excludedPopulation: users with pre-existing kidney disease should consult a doctor

cards.claim: Vitamin D inadequacy is highly prevalent among athletes, which can negatively impact bone health, immune function, and potentially muscle function.
practicalAdvice: If you live in a region with low sunlight, train indoors, or have darker skin, consider having your Vitamin D levels checked.
Supplementation may be necessary if blood levels are found to be insufficient or deficient.

source.title: Prevalence of vitamin D inadequacy in athletes: a systematic-review and meta-analysis
source.scope: Athletes; prevalence of vitamin D inadequacy and implications for health and performance.

limitations: Supplementation is primarily beneficial if a deficiency exists; excessive supplementation does not confer additional athletic benefits.

cards.claim: Overtraining syndrome is a severe condition characterized by a persistent, unexplained decline in performance despite continued training and adequate rest, often accompanied by mood disturbances.
practicalAdvice: True overtraining syndrome takes weeks or months to recover from; prevention through careful load management is critical.
If performance drops persistently over weeks alongside severe fatigue and irritability, consult a professional to rule out medical issues.

source.title: Overtraining syndrome: a practical guide
source.scope: Athletes; practical guidance on identifying and managing overtraining syndrome.

limitations: Overtraining syndrome is a diagnosis of exclusion and must be differentiated from functional overreaching or medical conditions like anemia.

cards.claim: Rapid spikes in acute training load relative to chronic training capacity (an acute:chronic workload ratio >=1.5) are strongly associated with an increased risk of injury.
practicalAdvice: Avoid sudden, drastic increases in training volume or intensity from week to week.
A progressive, controlled approach to increasing your training load builds resilience and protects against injuries better than undertraining.

source.title: The training-injury prevention paradox: should athletes be training smarter and harder?
source.scope: Athletes; training loads, acute to chronic workload ratios, and injury prevention.

cards.claim: For resistance-trained, lean athletes undergoing a caloric restriction to lose fat, dietary protein needs are elevated to 2.3-3.1 g/kg of fat-free mass to prevent muscle loss.
practicalAdvice: When eating in a calorie deficit, prioritize high protein intake to signal your body to retain muscle mass while losing fat.
The leaner you are and the larger the deficit, the more protein you need to protect your muscle tissue.

source.title: A systematic review of dietary protein during caloric restriction in resistance trained lean athletes: a case for higher intakes
source.organization: International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism
source.scope: Resistance trained lean athletes; protein needs during caloric restriction.

dosage.note: 2.3 to 3.1 g/kg of fat-free mass (FFM) is generally higher than standard protein recommendations.

cards.claim: Consuming carbohydrates alongside protein near the training window can maximize glycogen resynthesis and support prolonged, high-volume exercise performance.
practicalAdvice: If you are training intensely multiple times a day or doing very prolonged sessions, prioritize consuming carbohydrates immediately after and during workouts.
For a standard 1-hour lifting session, total daily carbohydrate intake matters more than exact pre- or post-workout timing.

source.title: International society of sports nutrition position stand: nutrient timing
source.organization: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition
source.scope: Athletes and active individuals; timing of macronutrient ingestion.

cards.claim: Muscle hypertrophy is theorized to be mediated by three primary factors: mechanical tension, metabolic stress, and to a lesser extent, muscle damage.
practicalAdvice: Focus on mechanical tension (lifting progressively heavier weights) as the main driver of your growth.
Metabolic stress (the 'pump') can be a secondary stimulus, but muscle damage should not be the main goal.

source.title: The mechanisms of muscle hypertrophy and their application to resistance training
source.organization: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
source.scope: Resistance trained individuals; mechanisms driving muscle hypertrophy.

cards.claim: Muscle hypertrophy is driven primarily by mechanical tension activating mTOR signaling pathways, not by microscopic muscle tears. Muscle damage is a training byproduct, not the primary growth mechanism.
practicalAdvice: You do not need to intentionally cause muscle damage to grow. Consistent progressive overload (mechanical tension) is the most reliable driver of muscle growth.
Avoid changing exercises too often just to 'shock' the muscles into being damaged.

source.title: Stimuli and sensors that initiate skeletal muscle hypertrophy following resistance exercise
source.scope: Healthy adults; molecular signaling and stimuli for hypertrophy.

cards.claim: Delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS) correlates poorly with muscle hypertrophy and is not a valid or reliable indicator of muscular adaptations.
practicalAdvice: You do not need to feel sore after a workout for it to have stimulated muscle growth.
Do not judge the quality of your workout by how sore you are the next day; track your strength progression instead.

source.title: Is Postexercise Muscle Soreness a Valid Indicator of Muscular Adaptations?
source.scope: Resistance trained individuals; relationship between DOMS and muscle hypertrophy.

cards.claim: Resistance training with low loads (e.g., 20% of 1RM) can produce comparable muscle hypertrophy to high-load training, provided the sets are taken near muscular failure.
practicalAdvice: You can still build muscle using lighter weights if you take your sets close to failure.
This is highly beneficial for periods when you need to avoid heavy loading due to joint stress or limited equipment.

source.scope: Healthy men; comparing low vs high load resistance training on muscle adaptations.
